title: Food in the rule
hookLine: grace, simplicity, maybe a fast day: the Torah puts the blessing after the meal, when you're full
tomorrow: a monk mocked praying monks as "navel-souls." who answered him?

lines: WHY SAVE THE THANKS FOR THEN?
cards: Heads bowed over hot plates, a quick thank-you, then forks. That's one way to say grace. The Torah's command puts it somewhere stranger.
Not before the meal, when you're hungry and the food smells wonderful. After. When the plate is empty and you're full and already half out of your chair.
Why would anyone save the thanks for then? Moses has an answer, and it's about memory.

teach.h: MAN DOTH NOT LIVE BY BREAD ONLY.
teach.b: It's in Moses's long farewell, in Deuteronomy. He reminds the people of the wilderness: forty years, hungry, fed with manna they had never seen, "that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only."
Then he looks ahead to the good land: wheat and barley, vines and figs, bread without scarceness.

teach.h: WHEN THOU HAST EATEN AND ART FULL.
teach.b: And here's the command: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee." After. Full.
Why then? The next lines answer it. Beware, Moses says, that when you've eaten and are full, and built good houses to live in, your heart isn't lifted up, and you forget.
Hunger remembers on its own. Fullness forgets. So the blessing goes where the forgetting starts.
That's why Jewish families say Birkat Hamazon, the grace after meals, often sung, sometimes long.
In Jewish teaching, the blessing after the meal is the Torah's own command, and the short blessings before eating come from the rabbis.
Both are kept now: a word before, a fuller one after. For a food practice in your rule, the Torah's order is worth borrowing. Not only thanks when the plate arrives hot.
A pause when it's empty, and you're full, and you'd rather get up.

how: Jewish families say Birkat Hamazon, the grace after meals, often sung, and short blessings before eating. A personal rule might include one food practice: a grace, a simple meal, or an occasional fast day.

games.q: what does “food in the rule” mean?
o: one food practice in your rule, like thanks after the meal
a list of foods the Bible forbids everyone to eat
a strict diet plan you follow to lose weight quickly

p: when the Torah says to bless
lest your heart is lifted up and forgets

s: in the Torah, the command to bless comes before eating
Deuteronomy 8:10: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless."
Moses warns that fullness, not hunger, is when people forget
after eating and building good houses, he says, beware lest you forget.
Jewish practice drops the blessing before meals
both are kept: short blessings before, and the grace after.

games.q: lunch at your desk, done in five minutes, already onto the next email. what does Deuteronomy 8 point to?
o: a pause after, full, to give thanks: fullness is where forgetting starts.
nothing: thanks only counts when you're hungry and the food is hot.
eat less, so you never get full enough to forget.
games.why: The Torah puts the blessing at the point of fullness, because that's when Moses says hearts get lifted up and forget.

practice: Take something small to eat or drink: a piece of fruit, a cracker, a sip of tea. Taste it slowly, all the way to the end. Then, finished and a little full, stay seated a moment longer and give thanks after, for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Food in the rule: one food practice written into your rule, like the Torah's blessing after the meal, when you're full.

orig.note: Hebrew: the blessing of the food, the Jewish grace after meals.

carryVoice: Your line: eat with care. The blessing goes where the forgetting starts. That's day 1647, and the table is cleared.
